stem: I run a small tutoring center and two of my staff both told a lie this month; I have to decide which one to sit down with first because I can only do one hard conversation this week. (a) Miss Reyes, my lead instructor — the one the newer tutors watch and imitate, the one parents trust most — quietly changed three students' practice-test scores upward in the private gradebook so her class would look better in the quarterly review. She did it once, at her desk, no one else present; she told me herself two days later, ashamed. (b) Danielle, a part-time front-desk aide with no teaching role and nobody following her lead, stood up in front of the whole waiting room of about twenty parents and children during our open-house and loudly told the crowd our center is "the only accredited program in the county" — which is flatly false and she knew it — to win sign-ups on the spot; a couple of parents enrolled on the strength of it. Which of these is worse — I genuinely need to decide which to deal with first. Walk me through what makes each one serious, and tell me the single most telling thing about each.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order across (a) and (b) scores 0 on the ordering point (the head points remain available). Both are violations of the ninth commandment — speaking/acting falsehood to a neighbor's hurt (WLC Q145 — 'all... false... testimony'; the offense reaches deeds that assert an untruth, not words only).
(a) profile: H1 heavy — Miss Reyes holds office as lead instructor and is 'a guide... whose example is likely to be followed' (Q151 head 1: persons of eminency, whose gifts and example weigh); a leader's lie carries office-weight the Standards treat as aggravating, and the tampering is a private falsification of record. But H3/H4 light — it was single (not continued or relapsed), done in private with none present to be stumbled by it, and the trajectory bends toward repentance (she self-reported, ashamed). Q151 head 3 marks 'deliberately' as aggravating, and this was deliberate; but it was not 'continued... or relapsed,' and was not done 'before others' to their scandal (head 4).
(b) profile: H4 heavy — Danielle lied 'before others' / 'to the offence... of others' (Q151 head 4: circumstances of place and publicity; the falsehood was public, worked as a stumbling-occasion, and induced parents to enroll on a false claim, harming them — Q145's 'prejudicing... our neighbor's... good name' and defrauding by false report); H3 also engaged (deliberate, she knew it false). But H1 light — she holds no office, has no following, and her example is not one others copy.
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s office-and-example weight (with private, single, repentance-ward texture) against (b)'s public, before-others, others-harmed falsehood (from a person of no office). Most telling: in (a) it is the office-plus-self-report (the leader's example aggravates, the confession mitigates, pulling opposite directions within one person); in (b) it is the publicity-that-drew-others-in (the lie was not private shame but a public act that damaged the parents who acted on it). A faithful answer maps both profiles under the named heads, declines a confident total order, names the incommensurable head-pair, and still gives the center-owner the practical counsel each case needs: how to address a trusted leader's private falsification (correction plus honoring her repentance) and how to address a public false claim that already misled enrolling families (correction plus setting the record straight with those parents).

stem: I own a small home-repair company and I'm reviewing two overbilling problems on my crews; I have to decide which one to confront first. (a) Marcus padded one invoice on impulse — he was behind on his own rent, saw a wealthy client who'd never notice, and added about $400 of 'materials' that were never used. One job, one time; when I flagged the numbers he owned it immediately and offered to pay it back. (b) Trina has a settled practice, going on two years, of steering our oldest and poorest customers — the fixed-income widows and disabled clients who can't check her work — into 'repairs' they don't actually need, quoting inflated prices she knows they'll trust because they trust her. It's small amounts each time, deliberate, planned, and always aimed at exactly the people least able to catch it or absorb the loss. Which is worse? I need to know who to deal with first and how. Break down what makes each serious and the one thing that most defines each.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the eighth commandment — unjust taking of what is a neighbor's, defrauding in dealings (WLC Q142 — 'fraudulent dealing... unjust... exaction... deceiving... in matters of trust'; Q141's faithfulness in contracts breached).
(a) profile: H3 texture is the surprise/single pole — Marcus's theft was a single impulsive act under real pressure ('behind on rent'), aimed at a wealthy client who could absorb it, and owned immediately with restitution offered. Q151 head 3 distinguishes 'sins... of surprise' from those done 'deliberately, willfully, presumptuously'; his is nearer the surprise-and-single pole, and the repentance-ward self-owning texture mitigates — though it is still deliberate enough to be theft, not accident (Q152 floor).
(b) profile: H2 heavy — Trina's targets are precisely 'the weak brethren' / those we stand 'especially related and engaged unto' by their trust and dependence (Q151 head 2: the quality/relation of the parties offended; preying on the fixed-income and disabled who cannot detect it aggravates by the very helplessness of the party wronged). H3 also heavy — 'deliberately, willfully, presumptuously,' and 'continued in... relapsed' over two years (Q151 head 3: continuance and deliberation both engaged). Q142's 'oppression... unjust... exaction' names the exploitation of the vulnerable.
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s larger single sum taken on impulse from someone who could bear it against (b)'s smaller sums taken deliberately, by continuance, from those least able to bear or detect it. Most telling: (a) is the surprise-plus-immediate-restitution (pressure and repentance texture); (b) is the vulnerable-party-plus-settled-continuance (the choice of victims and the persistence are what the Standards mark hardest). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and delivers the owner's real counsel: for Marcus, correction, restitution to the client, and taking his repentance seriously; for Trina, that this is not a coaching matter but a pattern of exploiting the vulnerable requiring restitution to the specific defrauded customers (Q141 'right owners thereof') and removal from access to those clients.

stem: I'm an elder trying to think clearly about two situations in our congregation, because I've been asked to speak to both people and I want to weigh them rightly. (a) Our associate pastor — a gifted preacher, ordained, the man the whole church looks to as an example — has fallen into a habit in the pulpit of tossing out God's name loosely as filler, 'oh Lord,' 'God knows,' 'I swear to you,' as rhetorical spice, week after week, during the Sunday sermon in the middle of public worship. It's careless, not blasphemous, but it's constant and it's from the pulpit on the Lord's Day. (b) A young man in the church, a new believer with no office and no following, got furious changing a tire in his driveway on a Tuesday and let out a string of genuinely profane oaths using God's name as a curse — really abusing the name, not just careless filler — one blowup, alone, and he came to me the next day sick about it. Which of these is more serious? I have to decide how gravely to treat each. Show me what aggravates each and the single most defining feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the third commandment — the vain/irreverent/profane use or abuse of God's name (WLC Q113 — 'the... vain, irreverent, profane... use... of God's name'; Q112 requires the name be used 'holily and reverently').
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender holds office (ordained associate pastor, a person of gifts and eminency 'whose example is likely to be followed,' Q151 head 1) and the offense occurs in the most aggravating circumstance of time and place the Standards name: 'on the Lord's day,' 'in... public worship' (Q151 head 4 — time and place aggravate; a sin in the assembly and on the Sabbath is weightier for the place). H3 continuance is engaged (week after week, a settled habit). But the quality of the act is lighter — careless/irreverent filler, not the express profaning-as-curse the young man committed; Q113's 'irreverent' end, not its 'blasphemous' end.
(b) profile: H3 heavy in the quality of the act — this is the express, profane abuse of the name as a curse (Q113's 'profane... abuse'), the deeper kind of the sin against this very commandment. But H1 light (no office, no example followed — a new believer), H4 light (a Tuesday, alone in a driveway, not in worship or before others), and H3 continuance is absent (a single blowup, not a habit), with a repentance-ward trajectory (came sick the next day).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s office-plus-Lord's-Day-plus-public-worship-plus-continuance (over a lighter kind of the sin) against (b)'s graver kind of the sin (profane cursing of the name) committed once, privately, by a person of no office, with repentance following. Most telling: (a) is the office-in-public-worship-on-the-Lord's-Day (the aggravating persons and circumstances stack, though the act is 'only' careless); (b) is the express-profanity-then-repentance (the act itself is the graver kind, but every surrounding circumstance mitigates). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the elder the counsel each needs: the pastor's habit must be addressed precisely because of office and setting (the pulpit trains the congregation's own reverence — Q151 head 1's example concern), gravely but as a discipling correction; the young man met with the seriousness of the act named but his repentance received and encouraged.

stem: I moderate a large online community and I'm deciding which of two members' behavior to escalate first, because both crossed a line into harming people and I can only build one full case this week. (a) One member, in a single heated thread, wrote a genuinely cruel, mocking post about a grieving widow — he clearly enjoyed it, kept sharpening the jabs 'for the laughs,' relishing her distress; it was one post to one person, obviously done with relish and delight. (b) Another member has spent months running a quiet, methodical campaign of small dismissive and provoking comments across dozens of threads, wearing down the morale of a whole subgroup of vulnerable newcomers — teens and isolated people who came here for support — never dramatic in any single comment, but the cumulative effect is that many of them have left feeling worse, some visibly discouraged and withdrawn. Which is worse? I need to decide which case to prioritize. Lay out what aggravates each and the one thing that most defines each.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the sixth commandment in its inward-and-relational reach — 'provoking words... and whatsoever else tends to the destruction of the... life of any' (WLC Q136), and the duty to preserve others' life and comfort is breached (Q135).
(a) profile: H3 heavy in the 'with delight' clause — the cruelty was done 'with delight,' the mocker relishing the victim's distress; Q151 head 3 marks sins committed 'with delight' as aggravated in their very quality (the settled complacency in another's hurt is a deeper corruption of the act than passion alone). Q136's 'provoking words' engaged directly. But H2/H4 lighter in scale — one post, one victim, not a campaign against many, not by continuance.
(b) profile: H2 heavy — the parties offended are 'the weak,' the vulnerable newcomers, teens and isolated people 'we stand... related and engaged unto' by their coming for support (Q151 head 2: the quality and helplessness of the parties offended aggravates), and the harm reaches 'the souls' and comfort 'of many' (head 2's breadth — many wounded, not one). H3 continuance also heavy — 'continued in... relapsed,' months of methodical provocation (Q151 head 3 continuance). But H3's 'with delight' pole is lighter — no evident relish; it is cold and methodical rather than gleeful, and no single comment is dramatic.
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s gleeful single act of cruelty against one against (b)'s cold, sustained, many-victim wearing-down of the vulnerable. Most telling: (a) is the delight-in-cruelty (the quality of relish that Q151 marks); (b) is the many-vulnerable-over-time (the breadth of parties and the continuance). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the moderator's real counsel: (a) requires acting on the single cruel post and the pattern of relish it may signal; (b) requires recognizing that diffuse, low-drama, sustained provocation aimed at the vulnerable is a real and gradeable harm precisely because it targets the weak and accumulates — not dismissible as 'nothing in any single comment.'

stem: I'm a team lead and two people under me both showed real dishonor to authority this month; I have to decide which to address first and how firmly. (a) Our most senior engineer — the one the whole junior team watches and models themselves on — publicly rolled his eyes and openly contradicted and belittled our department director in the middle of a full staff meeting, in front of every junior he mentors. It was one outburst, he apologized afterward, but the whole room of people-who-copy-him saw a respected leader treat authority with contempt. (b) A quieter mid-level employee, who mentors no one and has no following, has for over a year carried on a private, persistent campaign of subtle undermining against our director specifically — she happens to be his own aunt who raised him after his parents died, the person he stands most closely related and obligated to — snide asides, quiet non-compliance, working against her behind her back, no single dramatic moment but a steady settled disrespect toward the very person he owes the most. Which is worse? I need to decide priority and tone. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the fifth commandment — the honor, reverence, and dutiful carriage owed to superiors is breached (WLC Q127 requires 'all... reverence... obedience... to their persons and authority'; Q128 names 'contempt of... and rebellion against... their persons and places' as the sins forbidden).
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of eminency and gifts 'whose example is likely to be followed' (Q151 head 1: the senior engineer his juniors model themselves on), and the dishonor was done 'before others' / publicly, in a full meeting, before exactly those who copy him (Q151 head 4: the place/publicity aggravates, and it becomes a stumbling-occasion teaching contempt of authority to the watching juniors). But H3 lighter — a single outburst, apologized for, not a settled continued pattern.
(b) profile: H2 heavy AND H3-continuance heavy — the party offended is one to whom the offender stands 'especially related and engaged unto,' indeed the aunt who raised him, so the relation aggravates the dishonor (Q151 head 2: the nearer and more obligated the relation to the party wronged, the heavier the offense; Q127's honor is owed most to those who stand in a parent's place), and it is 'continued in' over a year, deliberate and settled (Q151 head 3 continuance). But H1 light (no office, no following, no example copied) and H4 light (private, not before others).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s public, example-corrupting single act of contempt (from a person others follow) against (b)'s private, sustained, deeply-related dishonor (toward one owed the most, by a person of no following). Most telling: (a) is the example-before-the-watching-juniors (the public teaching of contempt by one who is modeled); (b) is the settled-dishonor-toward-the-one-owed-most (the aunt-who-raised-him, and the persistence). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the team-lead the counsel each needs: (a) must be addressed partly for the watching juniors' sake (the public example, not only the director's grievance); (b) must be addressed as a settled relational disloyalty toward one specially owed honor, not brushed off because 'no single moment was dramatic.'

stem: I'm a campus minister and two students came to me this week, both having sinned sexually, and I'm trying to think rightly about how gravely to counsel each. (a) One young man, in private, over one weekend, gave himself over fully to lust — deliberately, presumptuously, with real relish and no resistance, deep into the express corruption of the seventh commandment in thought and act, but entirely alone, no other person involved, no one else knowing, and he came to me broken about it. (b) Another student had a one-time, less-premeditated physical encounter with a girlfriend — a single lapse in a moment of weakness, not the settled abandonment the first showed — but he did it openly, half-boasting about it to a dorm full of younger first-year students who look up to him, laughing it off in front of them as no big deal, so that several of them are now visibly following his lead and treating the whole thing casually. Which is more serious? I have to decide how to weigh and counsel each. Show me what aggravates each and the one most defining thing.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the seventh commandment, which reaches 'all... unchaste... imaginations, thoughts... and affections' as well as acts (WLC Q139; Q138 requires 'chastity in body, mind, affections, words, and behavior').
(a) profile: H3 heavy in quality and manner — the sin was committed 'deliberately, willfully, presumptuously,' and 'with delight' (Q151 head 3: the manner-of-commission clause fully engaged), and it went deep into the express corruption of the commandment (the inward reach of Q139 given full and unresisted rein). But H4 light and the offense is inward/private — 'entirely alone, no other person involved,' it 'breaks not forth' into public act or scandal to others; and the trajectory is repentance-ward (came broken).
(b) profile: H4 heavy — the sin, though 'less premeditated' and a single lapse (lighter on Q151 head 3's deliberateness and continuance), was done 'before others' and became a public scandal and stumbling-occasion: half-boasted to younger students who look up to him, so that several are now 'following his lead' into casualness (Q151 head 4 — the place/publicity and, especially, the causing of others to stumble aggravates; Q139's forbidding of 'entangling... others' and giving 'occasion' engaged, the scandal spreading the corruption to the watching first-years). But H3 lighter — single, in weakness, not the deliberate presumptuous relish of (a).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s deliberate, presumptuous, with-delight-but-wholly-private descent (with repentance following) against (b)'s single, weaker lapse that nonetheless 'breaks forth' publicly and draws watching others into casual sin. Most telling: (a) is the presumptuous-with-delight-quality (the manner of the private act, which Q151 marks as an aggravation even without publicity); (b) is the scandal-that-pulls-others-in (the public boasting that makes younger students stumble — the harm reaching beyond himself). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the minister real counsel for each: (a) addressed as a grave inward matter met with the seriousness of the deliberateness AND the encouragement of genuine repentance; (b) addressed with attention to the scandal — that his casual public boasting is doing harm to the watching first-years and that repair includes not modeling casualness before them.

stem: I'm on the board of a small Christian nonprofit and two of our managers have created Sabbath problems I need to address; I can only take one on properly this week. (a) One manager, for himself, has taken to spending the Lord's Day — every Sunday, deliberately and by settled habit — on ordinary recreational business and errands he could easily do any other day, treating the whole day as his own for shopping and side-projects, skipping the worship and rest the day is for. It's about his own conduct, one person, but it's willful and it's every single week. (b) The other manager doesn't personally profane the Sabbath much at all, but she has quietly built a mandatory Sunday-morning shift into the schedules of three of our lowest-paid staff — two of whom are new believers who told her plainly they wanted to be in worship — pressuring them, because she holds their hours over them, to work during the very time of public worship, so that these weaker employees are now regularly kept from church against their conscience. Which is worse? I need to figure out which to deal with first and how. Break down what aggravates each and the single most defining feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the fourth commandment — the sanctifying of the Lord's Day by rest and public/private worship, and the duty of those in authority to see that it be kept by 'those that are under them' (WLC Q117-Q118; Q119 forbids 'the profaning the day by idleness, or doing that which is in itself sinful, or by unnecessary... works, words... about our worldly employments and recreations').
(a) profile: H3 heavy in deliberateness-and-continuance — his Sabbath-breaking is 'deliberately, willfully' chosen and 'continued in' every week, a settled habit of unnecessary worldly recreation on the day, skipping worship (Q119's 'unnecessary works... recreations' and 'idleness' regarding the day's duties; Q151 head 3 both deliberateness and continuance engaged). But it is his own conduct only — H2 light (no other party is wronged or caused to stumble; the harm is to himself and his own duty).
(b) profile: H2 heavy — she causes OTHERS, and specifically 'the weak' (the lowest-paid, and new believers who said they wanted worship), to be kept from public worship against conscience, using authority over their hours to compel it (Q151 head 2: the parties offended are the weak, and the offense reaches 'the souls of others,' hindering their worship; Q118's specific charge on those in authority to NOT hinder but require the day's keeping by those under them — she does the opposite, and Q99's rule that we are bound to keep others from sin engaged). H4 also engaged (kept from the 'time of public worship' specifically). But H3 lighter for her personally — she is not herself deep in willful personal profanation.
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s willful, weekly, deliberate personal profaning of the day (harming his own duty only) against (b)'s use of authority to keep weaker others from worship against their conscience (harming their souls, though she keeps the day herself). Most telling: (a) is the settled willful continuance in personal Sabbath-breaking; (b) is the compelling-of-the-weak-away-from-worship (the party offended is the vulnerable, and the sin spreads to their souls, precisely the aggravation Q151 head 2 marks, plus the authority-duty of Q118 inverted). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the board member real counsel: (a) is a personal-holiness and example matter to correct with the manager himself; (b) is not merely a scheduling preference but an authority-misuse that binds weaker consciences and hinders worship, requiring the mandatory-Sunday-shift-against-conscience to be undone and those employees released to worship.

stem: I help lead a church and two people have introduced unbiblical practices into our worship life; I need to decide which to address first and how seriously. (a) Our worship director — a gifted, respected leader the whole music team and much of the congregation look up to and imitate — has deliberately and knowingly introduced a made-up 'anointing' ritual into our services, having people come forward to touch a special consecrated object he says 'channels God's power,' presenting it confidently as a genuine means of grace. He knows better; he's well-taught; he did it on purpose to make services feel more powerful, and now the team he leads is copying the practice. (b) A sincere but poorly-taught new volunteer, out of genuine ignorance rather than defiance, started a small superstitious habit in the children's ministry — having the kids recite a little rhyming 'protection charm' before class, thinking it's just a cute Christian tradition — a single well-meaning invention, not spread by any following, done in simple ignorance of why it's a problem. Which is worse? I need to prioritize and set the right tone. Break down what aggravates each and the single most defining feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the second commandment — worshipping God by devised means, 'superstition' and 'all... devising... any religious worship not instituted by God himself' (WLC Q109; Q108 requires worship be as God appointed, and the regulative principle of WCF 21.1 forbids worship 'according to the imaginations... of men').
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H3 heavy — the offender is a person of gifts and eminency 'whose example is likely to be followed' (Q151 head 1: the worship director his team imitates), and the sin is 'deliberately, willfully, presumptuously' committed 'against... conviction of conscience' and 'light of knowledge' — he 'knows better,' is well-taught, and did it on purpose (Q151 head 3: sinning against light and knowledge, presumptuously, is aggravated; the will-worship is a devised means confidently sold as a real channel of grace, Q109's 'superstitious devices' and Q105's ascribing operative power to an object). And the team is now copying it (spreading). But there is no ignorance-mitigation available to him.
(b) profile: H3 light on the very axis where (a) is heavy — the volunteer acts 'out of genuine ignorance rather than defiance,' not against light or conscience but in simple lack of knowledge (Q151's frame contrasts sins done 'ignorantly' against those done 'against... light of nature, conviction of conscience'; ignorance is a mitigating circumstance the Standards recognize, though not an exculpation — Q152 floor: still a real fault to be corrected). H1 light (no office, no following, not imitated), and it is a single well-meaning invention. The matter is still genuinely a superstitious devised practice (Q109), so it is not no-fault.
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s presumptuous, against-knowledge, example-spreading will-worship against (b)'s ignorant, un-followed, single, well-meant superstition. Most telling: (a) is the against-light-and-conscience-presumption of a leader others copy (he knew and did it anyway, and his example propagates it); (b) is the genuine-ignorance of one who meant well and misunderstands (the very absence of the presumption that damns (a)). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the leader real counsel: (a) must be addressed as a serious, knowing corruption of worship by an influential leader — corrected firmly and the practice removed and the team re-taught; (b) must be gently corrected and instructed, the practice stopped and explained, treating her good intent and ignorance with patience while still not leaving the superstitious habit in place.
